faq.a: Yeast is a living single-celled fungus. A spoonful of baker's yeast holds billions of tiny cells that wake up when given warmth, water and food.

faq.q: Why does dough need to be kneaded?
faq.a: Kneading lines up and links the proteins in flour into a stretchy gluten network that can trap the yeast's gas.
Yeast makes a little alcohol as it ferments, but almost all of it evaporates in the heat of the oven.

faq.q: Why does dough rise faster somewhere warm?
faq.a: Yeast is most active at around 25 to 35 degrees Celsius. In the cold it works slowly, and above about 50 to 60 degrees it is killed.
The holes are the bubbles of carbon dioxide made by the yeast, which grew in the oven and were then set in place as the bread baked.
asks: What makes the holes in bread?

facts: One gram of baker's yeast holds around 10 billion living yeast cells.
Yeast dies at about 60 degrees Celsius, so baking stops the rising and sets the loaf.

quiz.say: What gas made by yeast fills the holes in bread?
quiz.show: What gas made by yeast fills the holes in bread?
quiz.why: Yeast ferments sugar into carbon dioxide gas and a little alcohol, and the gas makes the bubbles.

wrong.0: Nitrogen is in the air but is not made by the yeast.
wrong.2: Yeast uses up oxygen rather than making it.
